detail.name: SR-GNN 'best MRR@20 on RETAIL (0.3252) and ZALANDO (0.2804) among all 13 models in Ludewig et al.'
detail.issue: On RETAIL, stan takes the best MRR@20 at 0.3638, well above sr-gnn's 0.3252. On ZALANDO, sr-gnn's 0.2804 is beaten by gru4rec (0.3069), sr (0.3043) and ct (0.2993) — it is not even the best neural model on that metric there.
detail.correction: SR-GNN had the best MRR@20 among the NEURAL models on RETAIL only. The paper's own text says: 'Among the complex models, the best results were obtained by gru4rec on all the measures except for MRR, where sr-gnn led to the best value' (RETAIL). No 'best of 13' claim is supportable on either dataset.

detail.name: GCE-GNN 'showed the strongest undesirable popularity bias of the GNNs tested'
detail.issue: Table 5 of arXiv 2312.16695 gives Pop@20 on DIGI: TAGNN 0.102 (highest, bolded) vs GCE-GNN 0.097 (second, underlined).
detail.correction: TAGNN, not GCE-GNN, shows the strongest popularity bias. The paper says 'two GNN-based models, namely TAGNN, and GCE-GNN seem to have a stronger and usually undesired tendency to recommend more popular items.'

detail.name: Session-KNN / SR-GNN latency attributed to 'Diginetica (32k items)'
detail.issue: The 13.9-14.7 ms and 27.5 ms figures come from Shehzad & Jannach 2312.16695, whose Table 3 states DIGI has 43,100 items and 216,134 sessions. The 32k figure is Ludewig et al.'s DIGI preprocessing, a different split.
detail.correction: Diginetica in the source of those latency numbers has 43,100 items, not 32k. Minor, but the catalog-size framing used to argue the 30ms budget is off by ~35%.

detail.name: RecSys 2025 claim: 'simple models beat every recent GNN on MRR and lose only 3 cases on Hit Rate'
detail.issue: That sentence is lifted from the abstract of the DIFFERENT 2023 paper (arXiv 2312.16695), which says the simple models 'outperform all recent GNN models in terms of the Mean Reciprocal Rank... and were only outperformed in three cases in terms of the Hit Rate'. The RecSys 2025 abstract says something materially different.
detail.correction: The RecSys 2025 abstract states: 'only the quite early SR-GNN model turns out to be superior in terms of accuracy metrics on one of the datasets', and that GNN performance 'varies largely across datasets'. The '3 cases on Hit Rate' finding belongs to the 2023 GNN-vs-kNN study, not the 2025 GRU4Rec/NARM/STAMP study. The attached 'random seed choice materially moves GNN results' is also a 2023-paper finding, not stated in the 2025 abstract.

detail.name: Hidasi & Czapp RecSys 2023: 'median 7% to 99%' performance loss across six third-party GRU4Rec ports
detail.issue: The word 'median' does not appear anywhere in arXiv 2307.14956, and no 7%-to-99% range is reported. The paper's per-implementation, per-dataset losses span roughly 0% to 99.63%, including best-case ports losing only 0-4% on some datasets (e.g. Yoochoose -1%/-0%, Coveo -3%/-3%).
detail.correction: The paper's actual headline is 'In the most extreme case, out-of-the-box performance is 99.63% lower compared to the official version', with per-implementation ranges reported individually (e.g. '75%-99% lower' out-of-the-box for one port, 'up to 19% lower' and 'up to 15% lower' for others). The '7%' floor is invented. The paper covers six third-party implementations on five public datasets, which is confirmed.

detail.name: 'SAGE (WWW 2026)', DOI 10.1145/3774904.3792356
detail.issue: The DOI is real but resolves to a paper titled 'Same Last-Item Confusion Unveiled: A Unified Mitigation Framework for Graph Learning in Session-Based Recommendation' (Jinpeng Chen, Jianxiang He, Yuan Cao, Huan Li, Zhenye Yang, Kaimin Wei, Xiongnan Jin, Senzhang Wang, Weiping Tu), WWW '26. The name 'SAGE' appears nowhere in the title or metadata I could retrieve.
detail.correction: The subject-matter description (same-last-item confusion, popularity over-recommendation, plug-in mitigation) matches the real paper. The acronym 'SAGE' and the specific mechanism 'contrastive dual forward propagation' could not be confirmed and may be invented or mis-remembered; cite the paper by its actual title.

detail.name: GRU4Rec original key result: 'RSC15 Recall@20 0.6322 ... and MRR@20 0.2693'
detail.issue: These two numbers come from two different model configurations in Table 3 of arXiv 1511.06939v4. BPR-1000 gives Recall@20 0.6322 (+24.82%) with MRR@20 0.2467 (+20.47%); TOP1-1000 gives Recall@20 0.6206 (+22.53%) with MRR@20 0.2693 (+31.49%). No single run produced both.
detail.correction: Report either 0.6322 / 0.2467 (BPR-1000) or 0.6206 / 0.2693 (TOP1-1000). Item-KNN baselines are correct as stated: RSC15 0.5065 / 0.2048, VIDEO 0.5508 / 0.3381; VIDEO Recall@20 0.6624 is the TOP1-1000 value and is correct.

detail.name: Mamba4Rec origin: 'Liu, Lin, Yao, Zhao, Zhou, Yang, Tang (Georgia Tech), RelKD@KDD workshop'
detail.issue: The paper's own author block (arXiv 2403.03900v2 HTML) lists Chengkai Liu, Jianghao Lin, Jianling Wang, Hanzhou Liu, James Caverlee — affiliated with Texas A&M University (and Shanghai Jiao Tong University for Lin). Neither the listed author names beyond 'Liu, Lin' nor Georgia Tech appear anywhere. No venue or workshop is stated on the paper.
detail.correction: Mamba4Rec is by Chengkai Liu, Jianghao Lin, Jianling Wang, Hanzhou Liu, James Caverlee (Texas A&M University + SJTU). The RelKD@KDD workshop attribution is unconfirmed by the paper itself.

detail.name: SPRINT (arXiv 2508.00570) identity and results
detail.issue: The paper is real: 'SPRINT: Scalable and Predictive Intent Refinement for LLM-Enhanced Session-based Recommendation', Lee, Kweon, Yue, Liu, Liu, Yoon, Wang, Kang, SIGIR'26 (v3, April 2026). But the survey reports two mutually inconsistent sets of results for it. The 'sequential' dimension says Beauty Hit@20 0.0577 / NDCG@20 0.0274 and that it LOSES Hit@20 to RLMRec-Con (0.0624), with inference 0.12-0.23s, '2025 preprint', 'no code'. The 'llm_rec' dimension says Hit@5 +49.9% on Beauty (0.0297 vs 0.0198), +55.4% Yelp, +136.4% Books, inference 0.12-0.57s, SIGIR 2026, 'code release'. The abstract states the method 'consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods', which sits awkwardly with the claimed Hit@20 loss.
detail.correction: None of the table-level numbers could be confirmed. The alias 'VELI4SBR' does not appear in current metadata and is unverified. At minimum the two dimensions must be reconciled before either number set is relied on; the 0.12-0.23s vs 0.12-0.57s inference figures cannot both be right.

detail.name: Speculative decoding for LLM recommenders: '2x to 2.5x' (arXiv 2408.05676)
detail.issue: The cited paper's abstract claims a '3-5x speedup' and saving '67% of computational resources'.
detail.correction: Replace '2x to 2.5x' with the paper's stated 3-5x. Note this makes the survey's own 'stack it all and you're still an order of magnitude short' conclusion slightly more conservative than it needs to be, but the cited number is wrong.

detail.name: MUVERA: 'FDEs retrieve 5-20x fewer candidates to achieve a fixed recall'
detail.issue: The abstract of arXiv 2405.19504 states FDEs require '2-5x fewer candidates', not 5-20x.
detail.correction: Use 2-5x fewer candidates. The companion claim, 'an average of 10% improved recall with 90% lower latency' versus PLAID, is confirmed by the abstract.

detail.name: WARP absolute latencies (171.3ms LoTTE Pooled, 58.0ms NFCorpus, etc.)
detail.issue: The abstract gives only relative speedups (41x, 3x). None of the absolute per-dataset millisecond figures, the index-size totals (95.51 GiB vs 190.52 vs 700.66), or the Xeon Gold 6132 hardware description could be checked.
detail.correction: The '58.0ms single-threaded on a ~3,600-document corpus' figure is load-bearing for the survey's central 'the model, not the corpus, is the cost' argument. It should be confirmed in the paper's tables before being used that way.

detail.name: jina-embeddings-v5-text nano/small scores and — critically — license
detail.issue: Scores are right (small 677M/1024d/32K/71.7 MTEB-Eng-v2/67.0 MMTEB; nano 239M/768d/8K/71.0/65.5). But both variants are released under CC BY-NC 4.0, i.e. non-commercial. The survey lists licenses in its summary as 'CC-BY-NC or Qwen Research (jina-v4) — jina-v4 being NC is a real blocker for a commercial portal', then explicitly recommends 'Use v5 instead' and closes with 'EmbeddingGemma-300m or jina-v5-nano at 256 dims int8 is very likely good enough to stop thinking about'.
detail.correction: jina-embeddings-v5-text-nano and -small are CC BY-NC 4.0 and carry the same commercial blocker the survey flags for v4. The recommendation to use v5 as the commercially-safe alternative is wrong. Separately, the claim that v4 is under the 'Qwen Research License' is doubtful — the v4 model card lists cc-by-nc-4.0. Also, the '119+ languages' figure applies to the small variant; the nano card states 15+.

detail.name: Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B MMTEB score of 64.34
detail.issue: The official Qwen blog reports 64.64 for Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, not 64.34. The figure is used twice, including as the comparison point for declaring bge-m3 (59.56) superseded.
detail.correction: 64.64. Dimensions (1024/2560/4096), 32K context and Apache 2.0 are all confirmed; the 8B score of 70.58 and 4B of 69.45 could not be read off the blog but are consistent with widely-reported values.

detail.name: SID model-scaling study (arXiv 2509.25522): '13M parameter ceiling'
detail.issue: The paper is real ('Understanding Generative Recommendation with Semantic IDs from a Model-scaling View', Liu, Collins, Tang, Zhao, Shah, Ju) and the abstract confirms the 44M-to-14B sweep and 'up to 20 percent improvement' for LLM-as-RS. But the survey's specific claim that 'scaling the recommender past roughly 13M parameters brings no additional gain' sits below the stated 44M floor of the sweep and could not be located.
detail.correction: Confirm the 13M saturation point in the paper's tables. It is load-bearing — the survey uses it twice to argue that a small model is not a compromise.

detail.name: GLIDE ablation figures (+25.0%/+29.9% Recall@30, R-KMeans +9.52%, greedy -27.07%, grounding +8.34%, 34% of recs, 21-day/~20M impressions)
detail.issue: None of these appear in the abstract and I could not reach the full text. The +25.0 vs +29.9 split is the single most decision-relevant number in the whole generative dimension — it is the survey's quantified 'price of anonymity'.
detail.correction: Verify these against the paper's ablation tables before relying on the '5 of 30 points come from persistent identity' conclusion.

detail.name: Netflix generative recommender (arXiv 2605.23312) production numbers
detail.issue: Paper and authorship confirmed ('Towards Generalizable and Efficient Large-Scale Generative Recommenders', Xu, Hsiao, Bhattacharya), and the abstract confirms a 1B-backbone beating a 2M-backbone across all reported tasks on 1M users. But the specific +22.5% / +11.3% / +7.4% relative MRR figures, the +28.1% cold-start number, the 'one-week shadow' framing, 'trillions of behavior tokens' pretraining, and the RecSys 2026 venue are not in the abstract.
detail.correction: Treat the three-task MRR breakdown and the cold-start figure as unconfirmed.

detail.name: GCE-GNN author attribution
detail.issue: The survey lists 'Wang, Wei, Liu, Liu, Zhang, Xu'. The paper's authors are Ziyang Wang, Wei Wei, Gao Cong, et al.
detail.correction: Third author is Gao Cong (NTU), not 'Liu'. The Huazhong University of Science and Technology affiliation for the lead authors and the CCIIPLab repository are consistent with the paper.

detail.name: LLMRank benchmark numbers (GPT-3.5 48.80 vs SASRec 78.89 NDCG@10 on ML-1M)
detail.issue: The paper is real and correctly attributed (ECIR 2024, Renmin University), but its abstract contains no numeric claims and I could not reach the tables. These numbers carry the survey's strongest single argument in the llm_rec overhyped section ('loses by ~30 NDCG points').
detail.correction: Verify the 48.80 / 46.74 / 78.89 / 17.88 (ML-1M) and 62.88 / 75.92 (Games) values, and note that they are computed over a 20-candidate reranking task, not full-catalog ranking, so the absolute magnitudes are not comparable to full-catalog NDCG figures elsewhere in the survey.

detail.name: Arctic-Embed 2.0 truncation ablation (MTEB-R 0.554→0.549 at 256 dims, competitor 94%/93%)
detail.issue: The paper (arXiv 2412.04506, Yu, Merrick, Nuti, Snowflake) is real, but its abstract states no numbers and the specific nDCG@10 retention table could not be checked.
detail.correction: The claim that MRL loss was applied during both pretraining and finetuning, and the 128-bytes-per-document figure, are also unverified. This ablation is used as the survey's cleanest evidence for choosing a compression-resilient model, so it should be confirmed.

detail.name: LinUCB (arXiv:1003.0146) — hybrid vs disjoint attribution of the +12.5% lift
detail.issue: The 'bandits' entry states: 'Hybrid LinUCB achieved +12.5% click lift over a context-free (epsilon-greedy) bandit at 100% data, and +20.1% lift at 1% data size.' Table 1 of the paper (deployment bucket) shows disjoint LinUCB at 12.5% at 100% data, while hybrid LinUCB gets only 8.4% at 100%. The two figures come from two different algorithms and have been fused into one claim about 'hybrid'.
detail.correction: At 100% data (deployment bucket): linucb(disjoint) = 12.5%, linucb(hybrid) = 8.4%. The abstract's headline 12.5% refers to DISJOINT LinUCB. The +20.1% at 1% data IS hybrid, and is correctly attributed. Note the 'production' dimension states the 12.5% figure without the 'hybrid' qualifier and is therefore fine. Confirmed: 33M+ events, +12.5% headline.

detail.name: TransAct V2 (arXiv:2506.02267) — '16,000 actions' and '160x scale-up'
detail.issue: The survey repeatedly claims TransAct V2 extends to 'up to 16,000, a 160x scale-up' (model entry), '16k lifelong actions' (production dimension_summary) and 'TransAct V2 (16k actions)' (overhyped). Two separate full-text fetches of the paper found neither figure. The paper states the lifelong sequence has length O(10^4) (~10,000) versus O(10^2) for the realtime and impression sequences, and makes no 160x scale-up claim.
detail.correction: Paper states lifelong sequence length is O(10^4), i.e. roughly 10,000 actions, versus O(10^2) for TransAct v1's realtime sequence — roughly a 100x extension by order of magnitude, not a stated '16,000 / 160x'. The rest of the entry is CONFIRMED: online A/B +6.35% Homefeed Repin Volume, -12.80% Hide Volume, +0.45% Impression Diversity, +1.41% Time Spent; offline +13.31% HIT@3/repin and -11.25% HIT@3/hide.

detail.name: BST (arXiv:1905.06874) — '+7.6% absolute online CTR'
detail.issue: The survey describes BST's gain as '+7.6% absolute online CTR over Wide&Deep' and repeats 'the published 13→20ms delta' framing. The paper's Table 4 reports a +7.57% online CTR gain, which is a RELATIVE improvement over the WDL baseline, not an absolute percentage-point gain. A 7.6-point absolute CTR increase would be implausibly large for a Taobao feed and materially overstates the result.
detail.correction: BST reports +7.57% RELATIVE online CTR gain over Wide&Deep. Everything else in the entry is CONFIRMED: average RT 13ms (WDL) → 20ms (BST b=1); offline AUC 0.7734 (WDL), 0.7866 (DIN), 0.7894 (BST).

detail.name: Dream11 Hierarchical Contextual Uplift Bandit (arXiv:2601.14333) — '+0.51% revenue (p=0.034)'
detail.issue: The paper exists (submitted 20 Jan 2026; authors Agrawal, Mohanty, Bhattacharjee, Mittal) and full production deployment in May 2025 is confirmed. But the reported figures are a 0.4% revenue improvement in the A/B test and a FURTHER 0.5% improvement observed after full production deployment. The survey's single combined claim of '+0.51% revenue (p=0.034) on the full population' does not match either figure, and I could not locate any p-value in the paper (the PDF would not extract; the abstract contains none).
detail.correction: Paper reports ~0.4% revenue lift in A/B testing, plus a further ~0.5% after full deployment (May 2025). The specific value '0.51%' and the p-value '0.034' are unsupported by anything I could retrieve. The survey's qualitative point (sub-1% revenue lift is the realistic magnitude) survives; the precise numbers do not.

detail.name: Embedding quantization deltas (-6.50 / -1.95 / -0.09 / -0.93) attributed to sbert.net docs
detail.issue: The survey cites https://sbert.net/examples/.../embedding-quantization/README.html for 'binary alone -6.50 points, int8 alone -1.95, int8 with rescoring -0.09, binary with rescoring -0.93', and builds a whole caveat around the -0.93 vs -6.50 gap. Two fetches of that page found no such table — it only states binary quantization preserves 'up to ~96%' of retrieval performance and defers to the HF blog. The HF blog (huggingface.co/blog/embedding-quantization) reports a different framing entirely: on mxbai-embed-large-v1, MTEB Retrieval NDCG@10 float32 54.39 → int8 52.79 → binary 52.46, with retention of 92.53% (binary), 96.45% (binary+rescoring), ~99% (int8+rescoring). None of the four cited point-deltas appear in either source.
detail.correction: Cannot confirm the four delta figures at the cited URL or the linked blog. Verifiable substitutes: binary retains 92.53% without rescoring and 96.45% with rescoring; Qdrant's '~96% retained at 32x reduction' is consistent. The survey's underlying argument (rescoring requires float vectors, so a pure client-side binary index does not get the good number) is directionally supported by the 92.53% vs 96.45% gap, but the specific numbers quoted should be replaced.

detail.name: Transformers.js WebGPU benchmark — batch-128 (1518ms vs 50,497ms) and three-machine batch-1 range
detail.issue: The survey's 'overhyped #1' argument — that the famous '100x faster' claim is a batch-128 throughput figure — rests on 'batch 128: WebGPU 1518ms vs WASM 50,498ms' and 'WebGPU 23.8ms / 32.4ms / 45.7ms across three machines vs WASM 386ms / 378ms / 507ms'. Fetching the cited discussion page returned only ONE machine (Chrome 122, Windows) with batch 1 = WebGPU 45.70ms vs WASM 507.20ms, and a maximum batch size of 32 (579.10ms vs 16,416.90ms). The batch-128 row and the other two machines' numbers are not retrievable at that URL (it is a multi-post community thread; other posts may exist but I could not confirm them).
detail.correction: Confirmed at the cited URL: Xenova/all-MiniLM-L6-v2, seq len 512, batch 1 = 45.70ms WebGPU vs 507.20ms WASM (ratio 11.1x, consistent with the survey's stated 'batch 1 speedup is 7.7x to 11x'). At batch 32 the observed ratio is ~28x, not 100x. The 23.8ms and 32.4ms figures and the entire batch-128 comparison are unconfirmed. The argument's shape holds; treat the specific batch-128 pair as unsourced.

detail.name: 'You Don't Bring Me Flowers' (arXiv:2507.16829) — 'RecSys 2025 Best Full Paper'
detail.issue: The paper is real and correctly described (conformal risk control for unwanted recommendations). The arXiv page states only 'Accepted at the 19th ACM Conference on Recommender Systems (RecSys 2025)' with no mention of an award. The RecSys 2025 best-paper-awards page returned 404. The survey asserts the award twice (model entry and overhyped section #4) and uses it rhetorically ('despite the award', 'RecSys 2025's best paper is offline on KuaiRand').
detail.correction: Cannot confirm the Best Full Paper award. Also note an author/affiliation slip: the full author list is De Toni, Purificato, Gómez, Lepri, Passerini, Consonni — the survey omits Lepri and Passerini and attributes origin solely to 'European Commission JRC / ECAT', when FBK/Trento are also involved.

detail.name: Netflix FM-Intent '+7.4% relative improvement in next-item prediction' and '+20% live engagement'
detail.issue: The survey presents +7.4% as 'the one concrete number in the lineage' and separately cites 'Netflix's RecSys 2025 live-content cold-start work reports +20% live engagement'. Neither is sourced to a retrievable URL (the entry's only link is the Netflix foundation-model blog post, which the survey itself says publishes no lift number). I could not locate the FM-Intent paper to verify; the arXiv ID is not given.
detail.correction: Both figures should be treated as unsourced until an arXiv/KDD citation is supplied. The survey's honest framing that the foundation-model blog itself publishes no lift number is a good sign, but it then leans on two unlinked numbers.

detail.name: Numbers not independently verified this session (default UNVERIFIED)
detail.issue: Budget-limited; these were not checked and should not be treated as confirmed: Open Bandit Dataset '26M+ click records'; ZOZOTOWN '>$3B annual GMV'; PI estimator's '10x+ RMSE, p<1e-8' and LETOR4.0 setup; DR-shrinkage '51 vs 21 conditions' and '86-90 of tested conditions'; MIPS+SLOPE 'beat IPS in ~80% of 150 bootstrapped runs'; PG-TS's Yahoo setup (~20 arms, 24,000 events); Cascading bandits (1502.02763) details; CRC's MS COCO 0.0996 +/- 0.0052 and the alpha - 2B/(n+1) bound; RAPS's 2.11 vs 9.78 / 2.00 vs 19.7 set sizes; SelectiveNet's 2.43 vs 2.89 at 90% coverage; tCRC's 67.86 / 27.50 set sizes; CPFT's +4.551% average and 48→27 set size; EODRec's 0.021s/0.012s vs 0.169s/0.081s and 29-31x compression; EmbeddingGemma's <15ms/256-token EdgeTPU and <200MB RAM (these are Google blog claims, not in the cited arXiv paper); MeMemo/client-vector-search/VecLite latencies (survey itself flags as vendor self-benchmarks); Gemini Nano's ~4GB weights, 22GB disk gate and April 2026 rollout; Airbnb's +21% CTR / +4.9%; SDM's +7.04% / +4.50% / +24.37%; Booking.com's 30%-latency-for-0.5%-conversion; Alibaba SIM (+7.1% / +4.4%) and MUSE (+12.6%); CHORD's 61.2-173.8x and 51.8% NDCG@10 on MovieLens-100K; Pinterest TransAct v1's +6%/+11%/-10% and '>20x CPU latency'; Dacrema et al. '11 of 12'.
